newsitem.title: CHILE: Norwegian leads in bid for Antarctic trek title.
newsitem.headline: Norwegian leads in bid for Antarctic trek title.

text.p: A Norwegian adventurer may soon become the first person to finish a solo, unsupported walk across Antarctica, but a rival trekker was hot on his trail, sponsors said on Tuesday.

In an unofficial race to be the first to accomplish the feat, Norwegian trekker Borge Ousland was well out in front and at his current pace would finish walking across the frozen continent in mid-January, sponsors said.
A Polish rival, Marek Kaminsky, who set out about the same time and place as Ousland was well behind him while a six-man South Korean group was not far behind Kaminsky, they said.

"Borge is doing extremely well. I think he's going to have a really good shot at it," said Lesley McGhee, manager for an adventure tour company that sponsored the walks and sends help in case of dire emergency.
Ousland's and Kaminsky's success makes it likely that one of the world's great, much attempted endurance feats will finally be conquered this year.

Ousland, making his second attempt in as many years, left Birkner Island near the Weddell Sea on the continent's Atlantic side, on about November 14 and reached the south pole 32 days later, said McGhee.

When he reached Amundsen-Scott Station at the pole, people at the base offered him a cup of tea, which he declined because to drink it would have cost his trek the all-important "unsupported" status, said McGhee.

He later left the pole and headed for the U.S. McMurdo Scientific Base, on the Ross Sea said McGhee, manager in the Chilean city of Punta Arenas for the Britain-based company Adventure Network International.
McGhee did not know Kaminsky's exact position but he had not reached the south pole. A French woman, Laurence de la Ferriere was behind him but she planned to stop at the pole, said McGhee.
